entries.title: A gentler introduction to everyday life
entries.summary: The authors suggest simpler surroundings and gentle, unhurried handling in the first weeks. They also recognize that a quiet home is not always possible, especially with siblings.
entries.cue: Your newborn is meeting the sounds, light and touch of daily life.
detail: Fewer visitors and softer lighting are among their possibilities for the first days, when family circumstances allow. A baby in a busier home is also getting to know the people and rhythms around them.
Their newborn-care discussion notices how much a change of clothes, a bath or a diaper change asks a baby to take in. They describe slowing the handling and keeping movements gentle.

In the interview with Karin Slabaugh, explaining an action before it happens and pausing to notice the baby are ways of showing respect. This attention is an invitation to understand the baby, without making a quiet change the measure of good care.

entries.title: Learning your baby’s feeding signals
entries.summary: The authors describe learning a baby’s feeding signals by noticing their movements, sounds and responses. The same cry can have different needs behind it, so these signs are possibilities to understand alongside responsive care.
entries.cue: You are getting to know how your baby communicates around milk feeds.
detail: Their examples include an opening mouth, whimpering or squeaking, tension in the mouth or body, and beginning to cry. They also ask what the baby looks at and how nearby sounds affect them.

They describe feeding a newborn on demand and gradually learning that baby’s rhythm. Their wider care discussion calls for a prompt response to needs; observation is part of caring, rather than a test the baby must pass before a feed.
In the same feeding section, they acknowledge choices, difficulties and specialist support when feeding is not going easily.

entries.title: Clothes that let your baby move
entries.summary: The authors favor soft, comfortable clothes that let a baby move easily. They look for an easy opening for dressing and a fit that is neither tight nor so loose that it creases or tangles.
entries.cue: You are choosing everyday clothes or noticing how an outfit feels as your baby moves.
detail: Wrap tops or a wider shoulder opening are among their examples. Their concern is how the clothes feel against the baby’s skin and how easily the adult can dress them.
They prefer simple clothing with few hard fastenings or decorations. Separate tops and trousers, with socks if needed, are examples they give for freer movement.
These are the authors’ clothing preferences, with comfort and movement at the center. Dressing itself can remain a gentle exchange with the baby.

entries.title: Bath time as a moment together
entries.summary: The authors describe bathing as gentle, supported care shared with the baby, with talking and eye contact. For a newborn, they explicitly keep the head supported throughout.
entries.cue: You are helping your baby through a bath.
detail: They describe familiar, economical movements and having supplies ready, including an open towel to receive the baby. A repeated sequence can help the adult handle the baby with confidence.
Talking, smiling and looking at the baby belong to the care in their account. Their emphasis is on gentle touch and adequate support, especially while a newborn is being handled.

references.locator: Gentle care, continuous newborn head support, prepared supplies and communication

entries.title: Gentle care when the car seat is needed
entries.summary: The authors call car seats essential for safety, even though seats limit a baby’s movement. They describe telling the baby what is happening and using gentle hands during this necessary care.
entries.cue: You are preparing to place your baby in a car seat.
detail: The book suggests attending to hunger and a needed diaper change before the trip. It treats being placed in the seat as something the adult can explain to the baby.
Participation grows with what the baby can do. The authors give offering an arm as one possibility, while the adult remains responsible for the care.

references.locator: Essential restraint, gentle explanation and participation appropriate to the baby

entries.title: Closeness and chances to move
entries.summary: The authors value the closeness of carrying a baby, alongside opportunities for the baby’s own movement. Their account includes an adult’s practical needs and changes as a baby begins to crawl or walk.
entries.cue: Carrying is part of your day, and you are noticing when your baby wants closeness or movement.
detail: They describe a carrier or sling as useful on public transport, at the shops or around the home. During the first weeks, they especially value the familiarity of being close to a caregiver.
They also make room for awake movement on the floor. As the baby begins crawling and taking first steps, they describe allowing those movements outdoors and keeping the carrier for longer distances.
Their carrier-selection discussion includes support for the adult’s back and room to accommodate the growing baby.

references.locator: Closeness, practical flexibility, adult support and movement as skills change

entries.title: When teeth begin to appear
entries.summary: The authors describe teething as easy for some babies and uncomfortable for others. Their account includes comfort and care for a newly emerged tooth, while their wider discussion keeps medical advice available for crying or pain.
entries.cue: You are noticing drool or caring for a tooth that has appeared.
detail: Keeping a cloth nearby to wipe the chin is one ordinary comfort they mention. Their examples of changes around teething are not a reason to assign every difficult spell to a tooth.
For newly emerged teeth, they describe cleaning with a soft cloth or toothbrush and water.
When crying is prolonged or a baby seems to be in pain, their broader care section describes sharing observations with a doctor or pediatrician and seeking medical advice.

references.locator: Variation between babies, wiping drool and care for newly emerged teeth
Observation, medical advice and adult support when crying or pain is concerning

entries.title: Connection while your baby is in intensive care
entries.summary: The authors describe ways of being present with a premature baby in an incubator, including talking or singing when the baby is awake and meeting their gaze. They keep the baby’s strength and response central to their examples of closer contact.
entries.cue: Your premature baby is in neonatal intensive care.
detail: Their account makes room for a familiar voice and eye contact even through the sides of an incubator. Connection is still part of the relationship when being together looks different.

They mention expressed milk when possible and forms of touch that attend to whether the baby is content or overwhelmed. Their example of holding the baby skin to skin comes only once the baby is strong enough.
This passage describes connection during intensive care; it gives no timetable for what a premature baby should manage.

references.locator: Awake voice, eye contact, milk where possible, strength and tolerance conditions
